Dāktūr Vōrthāt — The Lord of Metal

The Elemental Lord of Metal manifests in the celestial records as a figure of absolute rigidity and reflection—an official whose appearance never varies, whose rulings are issued in identical format regardless of circumstance, whose authority extends equally across all classifications of metal without preference or exception. Some Tānthëi scholars suggest that Dāktūr Vōrthāt does not merely administrate the metallic element but is the principle of hardness itself made bureaucratic: unyielding, reflective, and utterly indifferent to appeal.

Like all Elemental Lords, Dāktūr Vōrthāt answers directly to the Jade Sovereign (Vëizhük Dāknëi) rather than to a specific bureau overseer. His authority extends across all manifestations of metal—precious and base, worked and raw, decorative and functional. In the Tānvüri cosmology, metal is not merely a material substance but a category of being: the hard boundary that separates one thing from another, the reflective surface that reveals truth, the conductor of forces that would otherwise dissipate. Dāktūr Vōrthāt administers all of these simultaneously, maintaining the distinction between metal-as-boundary and metal-as-substance with obsessive precision.

The Classification of Metals

The Lord of Metal maintains the boundary between four primary administrative categories, each governed according to canonical protocols and subordinate clerk-spirits:

Base Metals (Vōrthāk Zhüt) — Iron, copper, tin, lead, and other common metallurgical materials. This category includes the raw ore in the earth (supervised jointly with the Earth Lord), its extraction and initial refinement, and its delivery to craftspeople. Dāktūr Vōrthāt delegates most routine supervision of this category to the clerk-spirit Zhütvōrthēk, who maintains the registry of all known ore deposits and their spiritual allocations. A mining operation that wishes to extract metal from a given site must file a petition through proper channels, requesting authorization from both Dāktūr Vōrthāt and the territorial Earth Official (Tūrvōr).

Precious Metals (Vōrthāt Fëk) — Gold, silver, platinum, and rarer metallic substances of ceremonial or commercial value. This category is supervised with particular strictness, since precious metals serve as the material substrate for the seals that authenticate celestial documents. A single falsified seal could theoretically compromise the integrity of the entire celestial filing system. For this reason, Dāktūr Vōrthāt maintains direct personal oversight of the precious metal registry and delegates its supervision to no clerk-spirit. Access to precious metals requires not merely a petition but a character assessment filed by the requesting party's household monitor (Zātkür) and explicit approval from the local Tūrvōr (territorial administrator).

Worked Metals (Höt Vōrthāt) — Tools, weapons, decorative objects, and ceremonial implements forged or cast from metallic material. This category overlaps with the Bureau of Transformation (Höt Sëi) and creates significant jurisdictional tension. The formal understanding is that Dāktūr Vōrthāt maintains authority over the metallic integrity of the finished object (its purity, hardness, and reflective properties) while Zhürhöt of the Bureau of Transformation claims authority over the functional transformation involved in the working (the forging, casting, and shaping). In practice, disputes over where metalworking ends and transformation begins are filed constantly with the Supreme Administrative Court.

Symbolic Metals (Vōrthāt Zhik) — Metal used in ritual contexts, ceremonial garments, temple furnishings, and administrative seals. This is the category most directly supervised by Dāktūr Vōrthāt in person. Every seal used in the celestial bureaucracy is registered in the Lord of Metal's personal records, and the spiritual weight of incorrect seal usage falls directly upon Dāktūr Vōrthāt's authority. For this reason, the Lord of Metal is intensely conservative in granting permission for new ritual uses of metal. Petitions to use metal in novel ceremonial contexts are frequently denied, on the grounds that unprecedented metallic symbolism creates unclassifiable boundary conditions.

Authority and Jurisdictional Tensions

Dāktūr Vōrthāt's primary administrative relationship is with the Earth Lord (Vëngdāk Zhütvōr), since all metal begins as ore in the earth. The two Elemental Lords maintain a formal protocol of coordination: Vëngdāk Zhütvōr authorizes the presence of metal ore within the earth's domain, and Dāktūr Vōrthāt authorizes its extraction and classification as separate from the earth-mass. This is theoretically clear but practically fraught—disputes over whether a particular ore deposit remains "part of the earth" or has been "classified as metal awaiting extraction" are filed with such frequency that a standing committee of the Supreme Administrative Court has been established to hear nothing else.

Dāktūr Vōrthāt's secondary tension is with Zhürhöt (Bureau of Transformation), over the boundary between metalworking and raw metal. This dispute is less formally resolved than the Earth Lord conflict, and Dāktūr Vōrthāt frequently files complaints that the Bureau of Transformation overreaches its authority by claiming jurisdiction over metals during the working process. The Lord of Metal argues that metal maintains its essential character throughout all transformation—a sword is still fundamentally metal, even when it is being hammered—and therefore remains under his jurisdiction. Zhürhöt counters that the function of the object determines its administrative category, not its material composition.

A tertiary administrative burden falls to Dāktūr Vōrthāt through his role in the celestial record-keeping system. The bureaucratic seals that authenticate all documents and petitions throughout the Tëngvōk Vān Lëi are metallic and therefore fall under his domain. Any disruption to the precious-metal supply directly threatens the administrative integrity of the entire celestial bureaucracy. For this reason, Dāktūr Vōrthāt petitions the Jade Sovereign regularly for expanded authority to intervene in mortal metalworking and mining—requests that are typically denied on the grounds that such direct intervention would violate administrative precedent. Nevertheless, the Lord of Metal maintains informal networks of influence through his clerk-spirits and through the priests of the Tānthëi caste who serve as intermediaries.

Mortal Engagement

Mortals petition Dāktūr Vōrthāt through formal offerings at temple shrines dedicated to the Elemental Lord, through the burning of spirit-documents requesting metallic prosperity or protection, or through the mediation of the Tānthëi priesthood. Petitions to Dāktūr Vōrthāt are characteristically formal and rigid—the Lord of Metal will not accept improvised or emotionally-charged prayers. All petitions must be filed according to established protocol, with correct spacing, proper seal placement, and unambiguous language.

Blacksmiths and Metalworkers form the primary petitioning constituency. A smith petitions Dāktūr Vōrthāt before beginning work with a new ore source, requesting that the metal comply with technique and expectation. Unlike petitions to Vōrjīk Jëk (the Fire Lord), which focus on the behavior of the flame, petitions to Dāktūr Vōrthāt focus on the integrity and responsiveness of the metal itself. A smith might petition: "Grant that this iron, being drawn from the Kērlüt mines and identified in the registry as Vōrthāt-grade base metal, shall maintain its purity through the forging process and respond reliably to temperature and technique." The metal's responsiveness to the smith's craft is understood as a celestial administrative grace, not a mechanical property.

Miners and Prospectors petition Dāktūr Vōrthāt for permission to extract ore from specific locations. This petition is theoretically filed with the territorial Tūrvōr (Earth Official), but in practice all mining petitions are forwarded to Dāktūr Vōrthāt's office for final approval. A prospector who discovers a promising ore deposit must first petition the Earth Lord for permission to disturb the earth, then petition Dāktūr Vōrthāt for permission to classify that ore as "extracted metal." Disputes over ore deposits between competing mining interests are adjudicated through the Lord of Metal's jurisdiction.

Merchants and Traders handling precious metals petition Dāktūr Vōrthāt for protection against adulteration and theft. A trader transporting gold across trade routes may offer to the Lord of Metal in hopes that the precious metal will remain unmolested and maintain its purity during transit.

Temple Officials and Record-Keepers petition Dāktūr Vōrthāt as part of routine maintenance of the bureaucratic infrastructure. New seals must be registered; old seals must be properly retired and recycled. The creation of new official documents that require authentic metallic seals flows through Dāktūr Vōrthāt's office, making the Lord of Metal a subtle but essential gatekeeper in the celestial administrative system.
